items.t: Anthropic vs Rolls-Royce: which shares have more potential over the next 12 months?
sum: Rolls-Royce (LSE: RR.) shares are probably the most popular growth investment in the UK. Week in, week out, investors pile into them due to the company's growth potential in areas such as defence, nuclear energy, and data centres.
The question is – do the shares have more potential over the next year than shares in AI powerhouse Anthropic (which is expected to IPO this month)? Let's discuss.
At first glance, Anthropic appears to have far more investment potential. Because the AI company is literally growing at an unprecedented rate.
In the first half of 2026, its revenues rose 1,300% year on year to $16.3bn. By contrast, Rolls-Royce's revenues only grew 25% to £11.3bn over the period.
However, digging deeper, the outlook for Anthropic shares post-IPO becomes less clear. For a start, it's coming to the market at a sky-high valuation of somewhere around $1.5trn to $2trn.
That price tag doesn't leave any room at all for a growth slowdown or operational setback. It's so high that it could fall even without a slowdown or setback.
Second, history shows that hyped-up IPO stocks tend to tank once the IPO hype wears off. We've seen this happen with both SpaceX and Cerebras this year.

Should I load up on Anthropic in my Stocks and Shares ISA in November?
sum: Anthropic has officially fired the starting gun on what should be one of the largest stock market listings ever. In a couple of weeks’ time (around 16 November), the maker of Claude AI is expected to IPO with a valuation between $1.5trn and $2trn.

This will follow SpaceX‘s historic stock market debut in June. I was initially sceptical about investing in Elon Musk’s rocket company, but I eventually did inside my Stock and Shares ISA. Could Anthropic tempt me to do the same?

Founded in 2021, Anthropic is one of the world’s leading frontier AI labs. It makes most of its revenue from metered token consumption. In other words, customers using Claude to do tasks like analyse lots of data and automate tasks.

Anthropic has a particular focus on safety and trust among enterprise customers. I like this. Once businesses embed Claude into their workflows, the retention rates are high, with many customers spending more money over time.
In its S-1 IPO prospectus filed last month, the company said it had more than 1,900 customers with $1m or more of revenue on a trailing-12-month basis, and roughly 250 customers with $10m or more.
Naturally, I would expect extremely strong growth from a five-year-old company targeting a $1.5trn+ valuation. However, the rate of top-line growth here is off the charts.
In the first six months of 2026, Anthropic’s revenue hit $16.3bn, a staggering 1,300% year-on-year increase. And there was a $974m operating profit in the second quarter.

Rolls-Royce stock gains focus after Hong Kong service milestone
sum: Rolls-Royce has reached a new operational milestone in its aftermarket business ahead of the company's next trading update. A report on the Hong Kong project says HAECO and Rolls-Royce completed the first local Module 52 swap on a Trent XWB-84 engine.

The work had previously required hardware to be shipped to distant maintenance facilities. Local training, tooling, materials and technical assessments could shorten aircraft groundings, reduce shop visits and improve fleet availability. That matters because recurring engine service revenue is central to the civil aerospace model.

The milestone does not by itself confirm the financial outlook. Investors will still focus on customer flying activity, supply-chain execution and the conversion of maintenance demand into cash. The latest analysis says the key test is whether Rolls-Royce can maintain its 2026 free-cash-flow guidance of GBP 3.8 billion to GBP 4 billion.

Rolls-Royce reported first-half free cash flow of GBP 2 billion, up 24 percent year on year, according to the analysis. The November update will show whether that momentum has continued through the remainder of the year.

The company also has longer-term support from its UK engine technology programme and a substantial order base across Civil Aerospace, Defence and Power Systems. Those factors strengthen the strategic case, but they do not replace near-term evidence on service activity, execution and cash generation.

Rolls-Royce's investor relations calendar lists the next trading update for Thursday, November 12, at 7:00 GMT. The real-time quote of Rolls-Royce stock traded at 15.35 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 18:10 CET on Monday, November 2, 2026, 0.07 percent below the Xetra close of 15.36 euros on Monday, November 2.

The official Rolls-Royce investor relations calendar sets the date for the next company update. Investors should watch the link between engine utilization, aftermarket work and cash generation rather than treating one technical achievement as confirmation of annual targets.

sum: Compared to the start of 2026, Lloyds Banking Group (LSE:LLOY) shares are virtually unchanged.
However, those thinking about selling up might want to take a closer look at the latest analysts’ dividend predictions.
The consensus forecast is for the bank’s payout to increase significantly over the next four financial years:
If realised, this would be a remarkable outcome. It would lift the yield on the bank’s shares from 3.7% (using its 2025 payout) to 8.6%, when the 2030 forecast’s taken into account.
Based on dividends paid over the past 12 months, there’s no other stock on the FTSE 100 that currently (1 November) has a higher return than this.
Indeed, an 8%+ yield’s better than anything that could be earned on one of Lloyds’ savings accounts. It also beats the return available on gilts (government bonds).

However, it pays to be cautious. After all, dividends are never guaranteed. And there’s little point buying a stock for its income potential if its share price is likely to decline over the long term.

£1,000 buys 1,113 shares of this cheap former FTSE 250 stock growing in popularity
sum: Card Factory (LSE:CARD) was given the red card from the FTSE 250 index back in 2019. Then the pandemic struck soon after, forcing the retailer to temporarily close all its stores. The share price duly fell off a cliff.
Since those dark days though, when the stock hit a low of 27p, Card Factory has quietly been trending upwards. Today, it’s reached 90p after rising 33% since January. So it’s gaining in popularity.
Yet the stock remains dirt cheap while offering a market-thumping dividend yield. So is this a potential hidden gem?

Many readers will be familiar with Card Factory’s high street offering of greetings cards and celebrations tackle (balloons, wrapping, decorations, paper plates, and more). Yet it also has a business-to-business division supplying the likes of Aldi, as well as a growing online operation that includes Funky Pigeon.

It’s also growing internationally. As such, Card Factory is becoming less reliant on just UK retail store sales. And despite the cost-of-living crisis, the firm is showing resilience. In the six months to 31 July, revenue rose 5.3% to £260.8m, boosted by strong digital sales.

Like-for-like store sales fell 2.3% as some consumers felt the pinch and stayed away. However, Card Factory is doing a good job at improving store product margins while investing for growth. It opened nine net new stores during the first half, taking the total to 1,126.
Adjusted pre-tax profit was broadly flat at £12.7m, while earnings per share (EPS) edged up 1.6% to 2.9p. Note that 83% of a £15m share buyback was complete by the end of September.

Rolls-Royce Rises 4.7% on Budget Hopes, but Execution Remains the Real Test
sum: Hopes for extra British defence spending lifted Rolls-Royce by 4.7% in the latest session, with Babcock International and BAE Systems advancing alongside it. The move was a sector-wide reaction to press reports rather than a response to any fresh company announcement — and that distinction matters for anyone weighing whether the stock's recovery has legs.

According to The Times, Wednesday's budget is expected to mobilise billions of pounds for British defence and military technology firms. City AM reported that Rolls-Royce and other defence names climbed on that prospect. The funding itself, though, is still a political expectation rather than secured revenue.

John Healey is reportedly set to channel additional money through the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank, with the capital aimed at defence-industry companies and domestic jobs. The Treasury confirmed on Saturday that the two public financial institutions will receive an extra £20.4 billion, to be deployed over roughly five years, with defence among the designated sectors.

Investors should keep the two strands apart: the recapitalisation of the state lenders is one thing, the defence commitments expected in the budget are another. What would count for Rolls-Royce is how that financing eventually feeds into concrete programmes and company orders.

The longer-term ambition is a path to defence spending of 3% of GDP by 2030. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates that reaching it would require an additional £17.3 billion in the 2029/30 fiscal year. Announced sums alone won't drive the valuation — their allocation and the delivery of the programmes they fund will matter just as much.

How demanding that delivery can be is visible in the American B-52J modernisation effort, which uses Rolls-Royce engines. A Government Accountability Office report dated 31 July found the CERP engine programme running 38% — or $3 billion — over budget, alongside significant delays. Bigger government budgets and programmes that stay on schedule are separate preconditions for commercial success.
Against that backdrop, the more durable case for the stock rests on signed business. Avolon's order, disclosed on 13 October, covers 70 Trent 7000 engines for 35 Airbus A330neo aircraft.

WWE legend Ric Flair shares health update following hospitalization
sum: WWE legend Ric Flair has shared his first health update since being hospitalized following a fall outside a Florida restaurant.

The 77-year-old wrestling icon was taken to hospital on October 23 after reportedly falling and injuring his face in Tampa. Two days later, Flair has reassured fans that he is recovering, while also addressing posts made to his Facebook account during his hospitalization.
In Instagram and X posts on October 25, Flair thanked fans for their support and the medical staff at Tampa General Hospital who treated him.
“Thank you all for the messages and prayers! I will get back to you each individually as I get stronger,” he wrote.
“Thank you to all the Tampa General Hospital staff and doctors that put up with me until 4:30am. I appreciate you all and thank you for everything you did for me!”
Flair added: “I am focused on my healing and recovery right now. I will be okay!”
He also addressed activity on his Facebook account while he was hospitalized, revealing that he no longer controls the page.

sum: It’s no secret that Rolls-Royce (LSE:RR.) shares have been phenomenal wealth-builders over the last three years. And that upward momentum has continued well into 2026.

Since January, the engineering stock has climbed another 20.4%, comfortably beating the FTSE 100‘s 5.8% return by almost four times. And it means that a simple £1,000 initial investment is already worth roughly £1,204 today.

Shareholders are undoubtedly quite chuffed with this market-beating result. But it’s important to remember that past performance never guarantees future returns. So the question now is, can this turbocharged business keep on flying?
Rolls-Royce’s growth isn’t concentrated into one single area. Instead, all three core segments of the business are currently on fire.

Airlines are ordering new, more fuel-efficient engines while also servicing their existing fleets. Government defence programmes are booming across Europe. And the massive AI buildout of data centres is fuelling demand for primary and backup power systems.
The result? Underlying revenue over the first half of the year is already up by another 26%, reaching £11.3bn.

And thanks to management renegotiating some of its older unattractive aircraft service contracts, aftermarket margins have significantly improved, resulting in a massive 46% surge in operating profits, flying to £2.5bn!

These targets, which relate to full-year 2026, imply a substantial step up from prior years and signal that the cost-cutting and pricing measures of recent quarters are flowing through to margins.

The updated guidance also provides a benchmark for investors to track execution. If Rolls-Royce were to deliver the midpoint of its adjusted operating profit guidance at GBP 4.8 billion, the upper end of its free cash flow range at GBP 4.0 billion would imply a free cash flow conversion of around 83 percent for 2026, a level that would compare favorably with many industrial peers. For investors, this combination of higher targeted profitability and strong cash generation is key to supporting deleveraging and potential future capital returns, especially in light of the company’s recent history of restructuring.

The same coverage from Ad-hoc-news highlights that Berenberg on September 14, 2026 reaffirmed its Buy rating on Rolls-Royce and maintained a price target of 1,900 pence, indicating upside potential of around 28 percent from recent levels near 1,486.00 pence.

sum: Rolls-Royce (LSE: RR) shares are quite frankly fabulous. This is the FTSE 100 stock of the decade. Everybody loves a comeback, don't they? We certainly got one here.

The great British engineering company almost collapsed during the pandemic. Global fleets were grounded and the lucrative revenues it generated from servicing aircraft engines on miles-flown contracts dried up. It's almost impossible to imagine today, but in October 2020 the shares slumped to just 39p. Today, they trade at 1,443p. That's a staggering 3,600% gain.
Anybody who bought around those levels and held on is in clover today.

Much of the credit goes to CEO Tufan Erginbilgic, who took over in January 2023. He immediately launched a transformation programme focused on costs, efficiency, commercial discipline and cash generation. It's worked spectacularly well.

In the first half of 2026, underlying operating profit jumped 46% to £2.5bn, while free cash flow rose 24% to £2bn. Rolls-Royce raised its full-year profit guidance to £4.7bn to £4.9bn and cash flow guidance to £3.8bn to £4bn.

Erginbilgic has now beaten expectations repeatedly and is heading for another year of strong growth. Despite that, the shares have slowed. They're up just 26% over the past year. That beats the average FTSE 100 return of 15.5%, but 29 UK blue-chips have done better.

The Rolls-Royce rocket ship had to slow at some point. And looking at the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, which now stands at 50, it isn't hard to see why. That's way above the typical FTSE 100 P/E of around 16, leaving little room for disappointment.

sum: Rolls-Royce’s (LSE: RR) share price looks expensive on almost every standard measure right now. The stock trades at higher price-to-earnings, price-to-sales, and price-to-book multiples than its major aerospace peers on current and forward estimates. Even discounted cash flow analysis shows the stock screening as 29% overvalued.
But crucially for savvy, long-term investors, this picture’s built entirely on guidance set by Rolls-Royce that it routinely beats.

The reality is that Rolls-Royce’s margins and returns have undergone a structural shift, so the old ratios give an inflated valuation picture. Consequently, the shares may still be significantly undervalued once the company’s true earnings power, growth trajectory, and transformed profitability are fully reflected.

Rolls-Royce’s 30 July-released H1 2026 numbers show the same valuation paradox playing out in real time. It issued conservative full‑year guidance earlier in the year, yet these results again blew past those forecasts. Underlying operating profit jumped 46% year on year to £2.5bn, underlying operating margins rose sharply to 22.5%, and free cash flow surged 24% to £2bn.
This level of over‑delivery forced the company to raise its full‑year guidance to £4.7bn‑£4.9bn of operating profit and £3.8bn‑£4bn of free cash flow.

These are well above the earlier forecasts that valuation models still rely on and imply an operational slowdown in Q2. That looks highly unlikely, given CEO Tufan Erginbilgiç’s comment that actions and investments the firm has made “will drive significant profitable growth to the mid-term and beyond.”
These results also underline how far the business has moved from its pre‑turnaround profile before Erginbilgiç became CEO in 2023.

sum: Rolls-Royce is deepening its exposure to the AI infrastructure boom, with the British engineering group forecasting that continuous power systems could account for as much as one-fifth of its power-generation business by 2030 as data centers struggle to secure grid connections.

CEO Tufan Erginbilgic said Thursday the company is already discussing power systems and small modular reactors with hyperscaler data center operators, and expects to seek internal approval for a major customer framework agreement.

"Early next week, in [the] investment committee, we are going to sign another big hyperscaler sort of deal," Erginbilgic said in a call with analysts. "We are already taking orders for data centers for [2028]."

Rolls-Royce is simultaneously benefiting from higher global defense spending, giving the company exposure to two of the largest investment cycles in international markets: the defense boom and the AI buildout.
In power generation, Rolls-Royce is seeing increasing demand for both backup engines and gas engines for use as a prime power source for data centers.
As a result, it now expects 25% annual growth in power generation revenue to 2030, up from a target of 20% previously, and up from less than 10% today.

Traditionally, Rolls-Royce sold mostly backup generators that sat idle until the electricity failed. Now, AI data centers increasingly want engines that generate electricity around the clock because they can't get connected to the grid. For Rolls-Royce, that means not only more engine sales but years of additional, high-margin maintenance work.

sum: Death and taxes. And Rolls-Royce (LSE:RR.) shares tearing to fresh peaks. Those are the three things investors have got used to counting on.

Risks to Rolls-Royce’s earnings soared in the wake of the Iran war. They remain elevated as the global economy absorbs the aftershocks. Yet the aviation giant has soared 26% in value since the start of the year. Be mindful, past performance is not indicative of future results. But to put that in perspective, the broader FTSE 100‘s up 7%, which is still a decent result in the circumstances.

And yet incredibly, some analysts believe Rolls-Royce’s share price is still too cheap. One predicts the engine builder will soar another 16% over the next year, to £17.40 per share. Analyst price targets are estimates only and are not guaranteed to be achieved. But if the analyst price target were achieved, a £9,999 investment in the Footsie firm would be worth £11,599 by next July.
But here’s the thing. There are 20 different brokers with ratings on Rolls shares today. And I’m more minded to listen to the collective wisdom of City analysts.
Their broad view? Investors today could lose a chunk of cash by investing here today…

The consensus among City analysts is that Rolls-Royce could slip 5% in value during the next 12 months, to £140.20. If that consensus price target were achieved, that would turn the same £9,999 lump sum today into approximately £9,499. Of course, these figures are illustrative only and are not a reliable indicator of future returns.

That’s not a catastrophic result by any means. Long-suffering Diageo shareholders like me, for instance have seen the value of their investments topple 17% over the past year. That puts the sort of mid-digit drop brokers are tipping into perspective.

It was trading at 1,480p today, July 7, after rising by 52% in the last 12 months. This article highlights some of the key reasons why the stock may continue rising.
Rolls-Royce share price may benefit from the booming air travel industry
Rolls-Royce Holdings is a major player in the civil aviation industry, where it supplies some engines that power popular wide-body planes like Airbus A350, A330neo, and A380.

The company makes money in two ways: selling the engines and entering long-term service contracts. In some cases, the company is usually comfortable selling some of these engines at a loss in exchange for these contracts.

Its servicing contracts are charged on a Power by the Hour approach, with the contracts lasting between 8 and 15 years. As a result, in this model, the Engine Flying Hours (EFH) is usually one of the most important metrics.

Rolls-Royce Holdings will likely benefit as the travel industry returns to normal following the US-Iran war disruption. In its recent statement, the management noted that disruptions did not have a material impact on its operations.
